title: SpaceX sued by Oregon and Virginia over AI deepfake porn, Grok safety claims
description: Jonathan Raa | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesLawsuits against Elon Musk's SpaceX are stacking up, with Virginia and Oregon becoming the first states to sue t
body: Jonathan Raa | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesLawsuits against Elon Musk's SpaceX are stacking up, with Virginia and Oregon becoming the first states to sue the company over issues with its Grok AI image generator.Versions of Grok and SpaceX's social network X have enabled users to generate and distribute explicit deepfakes based on real photos or videos of children and other people who did not consent, according to research by the Internet Watch Foundation, the Center for Countering Digital Hate and others. In separate complaints submitted to state courts as of Monday morning, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones argued that SpaceX failed to put safeguards in place to stop Grok and X users from making and sharing harmful deepfake images, especially alleged AI-generated child sexual abuse material.The complaints also allege that SpaceX has falsely represented its AI apps and social network (Grok and X) as generally safe, which the states see as a violation of Virginia's Consumer Protection Act or Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act. The matter is particularly concerning because X allows minors 13 and older to access its content.Rayfield and Jones both noted in their complaints that harms caused by non-consensual, sexualized images go beyond the victims depicted in the images."This content can cause fear, distress, and anxiety in those who are unwillingly exposed to the content," Jones wrote. Rayfield wrote that such conduct "erodes important norms regarding consent and privacy and trivializes sexual imagery, abuse, and exploitation."In a statement emailed to CNBC by a spokesperson for SpaceXSI, and posted on the company's @Safety account on X, the company said, "When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement. Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors."At an NYC Council hearing in October, a SpaceX AI policy leader, Gabriela Castillo Madrid, said the company had appropriate "safeguards" and "strict controls" in place around its AI products.SpaceX was already facing multiple Grok- and X-related lawsuits, and government probes around the world, including by authorities in the U.K., Spain, Ireland, France and the state of California. In private-sector lawsuits filed against SpaceX in the U.S. concerning Grok and AI-generated, explicit images, litigation is still in early stages and is tracked by The Center for Internet Technology Addiction.When the city of Baltimore sued xAI, now owned and operated by SpaceX, the company argued that under Section 230, they were not liable for unwanted images. Section 230 is a federal law that largely shields online platforms from liability for users' content.SpaceX also sued a user in a federal court in the Northern District of Texas for breach of contract after he allegedly used Grok to create and distribute deepfake explicit images, including depictions of minors. Lawyers for Musk's company argued that Grok should be seen as "a neutral tool, subject to user control," and that any image generation "is the result of the user's prompts and directions." The new state suits add to legal pressure on SpaceX. Both Virginia and Oregon are seeking injunctions, civil penalties, disgorgement and legal costs, while Virginia is also seeking restitution for consumers from Musk's company. Oregon submitted its complaint to the Multnomah County Circuit Court on Sunday evening, and Virginia submitted its complaint to the City of Richmond Circuit Court Monday morning. As of early Monday, the suits were pending the courts' acceptance.State attorneys general have recently succeeded in compelling U.S. social media companies to change their products and pay for alleged past harms.In August, for example, Meta settled a major federal case centered on allegations that the social media giant misrepresented the level of child mental health problems caused by its apps, Facebook and Instagram. Without admitting to wrongdoing, Meta agreed to pay states around $17 billion over a 10-year period and to make app changes that experts believe will help keep children safer online.

schema.headline: SpaceX sued by Oregon and Virginia over AI deepfake porn, Grok safety claims

title: ESPN, NFL to show Super Bowl 61 in Imax theaters
description: Moviegoers watch the film "Ne Zha 2" at an Imax GT Cinema on in Guiyang, China, Feb. 23, 2025.China News Service | China News Service | Getty ImagesSu
body: Moviegoers watch the film "Ne Zha 2" at an Imax GT Cinema on in Guiyang, China, Feb. 23, 2025.China News Service | China News Service | Getty ImagesSuper Bowl 61 will be telecast live in hundreds of Imax theaters in February via a partnership with the NFL and Disney's ESPN, which has the broadcast rights to the 2027 game. It marks the largest Imax live event in the company's history and the first time that the Super Bowl will be available in the format, according to a news release. The four-hour event on Feb. 14 will include ESPN's main Super Bowl game telecast, as well as Jay-Z's halftime performance and pregame and postgame coverage. Tickets will be available for theaters in the United States and select international markets, including Australia, New Zealand and Brazil. Tickets are expected to go on sale in January. Pricing was not disclosed. "Watching the Super Bowl with your fellow fans is one of the great shared experiences in sports, and this first-of-its-kind collaboration with the NFL and IMAX takes it to a historic new scale," said Ken Potrock, president of major event integration for The Walt Disney Company.In addition to ESPN channels, this season's championship game will also be available on streaming platform Disney+ as well as Disney's broadcast network ABC.

schema.headline: ESPN, NFL to show Super Bowl 61 in Imax theaters

title: Stop agonizing over the ‘right’ choice—to avoid regret, save time and reduce stress, take these 3 steps
description: If you want to be successful in your career, your ability to make a decision, map out a plan and take swift action is crucial. In 70% of the 20 fastes
body: If you want to be successful in your career, your ability to make a decision, map out a plan and take swift action is crucial. In 70% of the 20 fastest-growing occupations, as identified by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, judgment and decision-making are considered key soft skills, according to a ResumeNow report published Nov. 12. A November 2025 report from the Burning Glass Institute found that decision-making skills — including problem-solving, risk analysis and strategic thinking — were "one of the most enduring and economically valuable human capabilities" in the age of artificial intelligence, with 41% of more than 6.8 million U.S. job postings from 2022 to 2024 explicitly mentioning them. When the time comes to make an important decision, you naturally want to get it right. So you might research, examine every variable and analyze the data, only to find yourself completely unable to move forward. This analysis paralysis is often rooted in perfectionism, as you tell yourself: "I need to make the absolute best choice…" The problem with this mindset is that there's no such thing as a perfect choice. As a cognitive behavioral psychotherapist who specializes in anxiety and works with high performers, I know that maximizing — the never-ending quest to find a flawless or ideal choice — is a trap. In my experience, the happiest and most successful professionals don't waste time hunting for a flawless path or agonize over making the "right" decision. They pick a direction and channel their energy into making that decision work. The problem with maximizingLandmark research by psychologist Barry Schwartz, author of "The Paradox of Choice," and his colleagues shows that "maximizers" who obsess over finding the single best option end up experiencing higher levels of regret and depression and lower well-being than "satisficers," who settle on a solid choice that meets their core standards. Maximizing squanders precious time, energy and resources, and leads to choice overload, elevated anxiety and lower overall satisfaction. Coming from a cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) perspective — where the core idea is that our thoughts affect how we feel, our feelings affect how we behave and our behaviors reinforce our thoughts — maximizing is rooted in unhelpful thinking styles called cognitive distortions. These patterned, habitual ways of thinking aren't necessarily based on fact, but feel compellingly true. Specifically, maximizers get caught in black-and-white thinking, where a choice is framed as strictly good or bad, right or wrong, smart or dumb, and in catastrophizing, which means focusing exclusively on the absolute worst-case scenario. These rigid, all-or-nothing thought patterns and worst-case predictions directly fuel chronic anxiety, emotional paralysis and avoidant behavior, according to foundational CBT research by Aaron Beck and Judith Beck. For example, a maximizer might spiral down this road: "If I don't make the perfect choice, I'll get fired and lose my reputation, and Brad will get my office!" The reality? Initial decisions rarely need to be as set in stone as we might imagine. Success is rarely about choosing the single "correct" door on the first try. It's determined by making a sound decision and executing it with a flexible, dedicated approach. To avoid the maximizing trap, take these steps:1. Establish 'good enough' criteria Maximizing is appealing because it gives you the illusion of productivity; you feel like you're working hard by pouring energy into finding the single right choice. In reality, exhaustive research can be a waste of time and mental energy.This is why establishing "good enough" criteria is essential, based on Nobel Prize-winning economist Herbert Simon's concept of satisficing. It may feel risky at first, especially if your decision-making is being hijacked by catastrophic thoughts about worst-case scenarios. But over-analyzing is actually the riskier path. Start by identifying the non-negotiable criteria for success. Then make a rule that you'll spend no more than two hours on background research, consult only three resources or review just two or three vendor proposals. Once an option meets, say, 80% to 90% of your benchmarks, shut down the search phase and lock in your decision. Save the rest of your energy for planning and execution. 2. Set a decision deadline and stick to it Indecision and its close cousin, procrastination, function as avoidance strategies I see people use to temporarily escape short-term stress and anxiety. Time fuels analysis paralysis, and your options will feel endless if you don't set boundaries. Psychological research on procrastination confirms that delaying decisions can be an emotional regulation strategy rather than a time-management issue.To manage this anxiety loop, set a strict deadline on your calendar and commit to making a call once time is up. You can also create smaller time goals for different phases of the process, such as data gathering and resource identification. Remind yourself: A solid, well-executed decision made today beats a perfect decision delayed until next month. 3. Commit to flexibility Every decision you make will eventually be subject to change. The more valuable skill isn't finding the ultimate answer, but cultivating flexibility and adaptability. Clinical research on psychological flexibility shows that the ability to adapt your thinking and pivot in real time is associated with lower anxiety and greater resilience under pressure. When you learn to shift your focus from pre-decision evaluation to post-decision adaptability, you can make almost any sound choice the right choice. When you have thoughts like "I have to make the right choice," try to reframe them by asking yourself instead: "How will I pivot if this doesn't go according to plan?" It makes sense to want to get things right from the start. But even the most successful people aren't fortune tellers. So instead of front-loading the task by pouring valuable time and energy into maximizing, top performers save their precious resources for execution — and have the confidence to know they can handle the outcomes as they unfold. Chamin Ajjan, LCSW, A-CBT, CST is the CEO and Clinical Director of Chamin Ajjan Psychotherapy, a regional clinic of the National Social Anxiety Center where she is also a board member. She completed her undergraduate work at the University of California, Berkeley, and graduate school at Columbia University School of Social Work. She is also the author of "Seeking Soulmate: Ditch The Dating Game and Find Real Connection.″

title: ‘This establishes a bottom’: Jensen Huang’s return seen as likely to stop market sell-off, for now
description: Traders work at the New York Stock Exchange on Nov. 17, 2026. NYSEThe major averages of U.S. equities surged on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen
body: Traders work at the New York Stock Exchange on Nov. 17, 2026. NYSEThe major averages of U.S. equities surged on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, giving investors some hope that the relentless selling pressure seen last week may subside — at least temporarily.The relief rally came after the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite ended Friday's session in correction territory. The S&P alone tumbled more than 9% after Huang's departure from the chipmaker was initially announced on Nov. 12 through Friday. That sell-off may be over — at least temporarily — according to Wall Street experts. But key questions linger around Nvidia and the artificial intelligence trade that has carried the bull market. "I think the AI trade is back on," said Mark Gibbens, founder of Gibbens Capital Management. "I certainly believe this establishes a bottom and a floor in the AI trade and the recent market weakness."He added that the news likely doesn't alleviate all concerns that have driven recent declines, including worries about data center approvals after the midterms and fears that the capital expenditures cycle may have peaked. But Gibbens thinks the "keystone" role that Nvidia plays in both financing the AI buildout and the technology's supply chain means a more stable picture of the chipmaker creates a brighter view of the overall market than before. An encouraging sign that the correction may be over came even before Nvidia's Monday announcement, according to Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth Management. He said Friday's selling, which was indiscriminate and affected sectors beyond just AI-exposed companies, showed a bottom may have been building. "Sometimes you just hit that crescendo where you know the market gets oversold, and I would argue that we'd be higher today, even without the Nvidia news," he said. Indeed, futures tied to the major stock indexes were broadly higher on Sunday night, before any news regarding Huang's return. "So I think that sort of signals we've likely found a place where we priced in, at least the near term, as much of the bad news that was giving markets jitters over the course of the last several weeks."Strengthening the case for a bottom was that the technology sector's forward earnings valuation was cheaper than that of consumer staples, Hogan said. The S&P 500 consumer staples sector trades at a 20.5 multiple, per FactSet. Tech, meanwhile, trades at 16.3 times forward earnings. Hogan said that discrepancy doesn't square with the earnings outlook for the former sector. Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets, said Huang's return created a relief rally for a market that was oversold. But he's not sure the headline alone can get the market out of its funk. "I think the rally will probably fizzle out because now people will pull back and still have the same questions we had before he was replaced," Woods said. Those questions will likely play out in congressional hearings, he speculated. "The market needed this jolt to get us back on our feet, but it is still a counter trend rally in an otherwise near-term downtrend."Woods, though, said that the lows for the year are likely in, thanks to Friday's wash-out that spread to all sectors beyond those dependent on Nvidia's role in AI. While investors celebrated Huang's return, the sell-off that accelerated after his departure started before worries about his position even began. That stemmed from concerns about financing the buildout, data center approvals after Democratic wins in the midterm elections and worries that hyperscaler capex may have already peaked or is about to. That's why Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at One Point BFG Wealth Partners, is still nervous about the "picks and shovels" companies involved in the AI trade, a group he says includes Nvidia. "We should enjoy this rally, and maybe it lasts a bit, but I think that picks and shovels trade is going to be solely dependent on what that rate of capex spend is going to be," he said. "That, at the end of the day, is the story that those companies are going to have to deal with outside of bounces like we're seeing now."Traders at Goldman Sachs put it more succinctly."Not sure yet whether good or bad that the fate of the market is almost equal to the fate of one person. But hey ... We are not picky here," they said.— CNBC's Michelle Fox and Deena Zaidi contributed reporting

schema.headline: ‘This establishes a bottom’: Jensen Huang’s return seen as likely to stop market sell-off, for now

title: Trump hosts crypto gala as his meme coin falls below $1
description: MANILA, PHILIPPINES - NOVEMBER 18: U.S. President Donald Trump takes part in arrival honors with Philippine President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr.
body: MANILA, PHILIPPINES - NOVEMBER 18: U.S. President Donald Trump takes part in arrival honors with Philippine President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. )Ezra Acayan | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesU.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday hosted his third cryptocurrency gala for top holders of his meme coin, $TRUMP, which has plummeted to below $1 a coin after reaching a high of $75 the day before Trump's second inauguration, on Jan. 19, 2025.The dinner, held at the Trump National golf club in Sterling, Virginia, comes as some Democrats say they will investigate potential conflicts of interest and accuse Trump of using the presidency to boost his personal wealth.At Sunday's dinner, Trump maintained that his support for cryptocurrencies was to boost American economic competitiveness."I'm doing it for the United States ... If we don't do it, China's going to do it," he told attendees, The Guardian reported. The event also featured speeches from boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary and NBA champion Tristan Thompson.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconTrump Media shares have lost more than 60% of their value over the last 12 months. A total of 185 "wallets" met the criteria for entry to the gala, although the leaderboard on the $TRUMP coin club website listed just 130 wallets. The wallets listed on the leaderboard held $8.6 million in $TRUMP tokens, a sharp decline from the May 2025 gala, which featured 220 attendees holding a combined $148 million. Crypto billionaire Justin Sun's wallet alone held $18.5 million at the 2025 event — more than the combined holdings of this year's attendees.Eligibility was based on time-weighted holdings of Trump's meme coins from Sept. 30 to Nov. 16, according to the organizer's website. The top 29 holders were invited to a VIP reception with the president, with the top four receiving an 18-karat, Trump-branded gold watch.More than half of the wallets that qualified for the event were linked to crypto exchanges that bar U.S.-based users, according to data gathered by consumer advocacy group Public Citizen for Reuters, suggesting they belong to foreign nationals.The $TRUMP token has earned the Trump family at least $635 million, according to the president's June financial disclosure. Including the meme coins, the Trump family has earned $2.3 billion from its four main crypto-related businesses since the president's second term began, through to April of this year, according to a Reuters report.This is despite the ventures' falling value, which, according to the report, they invest little to no money in. Trump's stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group, is worth about $430 million as of Friday's close.Bitcoin regains groundBitcoin climbed back to over $61,000 on Monday in line with the U.S. stock futures bounce, after an AI-related stock sell-off spilled over into other riskier assets last week.Bitcoin fell as low as $55,130 on Saturday, its lowest level since September 2024. The sell-off wiped out $1.8 billion in leveraged crypto positions, largely from bets on prices rising. Leveraged buyers were forced out as prices fell, then returned after the price stabilized.The world's largest cryptocurrency is still trading at less than half of its October 2025 value. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost $1.24 billion last week, their third week of outflows, according to SoSo Value data cited by FxPro.

schema.headline: Trump hosts crypto gala as his meme coin falls below $1

title: Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’ sparks FTX portrayal debate among crypto bigwigs from CZ to Star Xu
description: NEW YORK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 19: (L-R) Anthony Boyle, Julia Garner and Graham Moore attend Netflix's "The Altruists" New York Premiere at The Plaza H
body: NEW YORK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 19: (L-R) Anthony Boyle, Julia Garner and Graham Moore attend Netflix's "The Altruists" New York Premiere at The Plaza Hotel on November 19, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Arturo Holmes/WireImage)Arturo Holmes | Wireimage | Getty ImagesNetflix's "The Altruists," released Nov. 19, has sparked backlash from prominent cryptocurrency industry figures, including Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, over its portrayal of the collapse of FTX.Critics have questioned the accuracy of the series' portrayal of the FTX collapse, particularly how it assigns responsibility of the scandal. Several crypto industry figures argue that it softens the culpability of Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison while casting Zhao — widely known as CZ — as an outsized villain.Zhao criticized the series in a post on X, calling it "insane" and questioning whether the show was intended to influence public perception. He declined to comment to CNBC beyond his social-media posts. Zhao pleaded guilty in 2023 to failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program at Binance, in violation of the U.S. Bank Secrecy Act, in a case separate from the FTX fraud. He was sentenced to four months in prison in 2024 and pardoned by President Donald Trump in October 2025.FTX filed for bankruptcy in November 2022 after a liquidity crisis exposed deep financial problems at the exchange. Investigations later found that billions of dollars in customer funds had been diverted to Alameda Research.Shortly before FTX's collapse, Zhao announced that Binance would liquidate its remaining holdings of FTT, FTX's native token, intensifying pressure on the exchange.Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison in March 2024 after being convicted of fraud and conspiracy charges. Ellison pleaded guilty to fraud and conspiracy, and later cooperated with prosecutors, according to the Justice Department.Crypto commentator Kaleo wrote on X that the series portrayed Bankman-Fried and Ellison as having been pressured and groomed by Zhao into committing their alleged crimes, while casting Zhao as the figure who orchestrated the scandal."Whoever wrote this script is shameless," Kaleo added. He identifies himself as a co-founder of NFT project LedgArt.Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin said in a reply on X that the show exaggerated Zhao's accent to the point of raising questions about whether the portrayal was racist.Meanwhile, Tigran Gambaryan, a former Binance executive and U.S. federal agent, commented on LinkedIn that the series downplayed Bankman-Fried's responsibility while portraying Zhao as a "cartoonish villain," undermining the showrunners' credibility.Binance co-founder Yi He criticized the series for portraying its characters as "one-dimensional" and "stereotyped," while suggesting that it shifted blame away from those responsible for FTX's collapse. She compared the show unfavorably with Chinese short-form drama platform Hongguo, saying Netflix "might as well be canceled."Changpeng Zhao, co-founder of Binance Holdings Ltd., during the Bitcoin Asia conference in Hong Kong, China, on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. Chan Long Hei | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBut the reactions were not uniformly supportive of Zhao.In a post on X, OKX founder Star Xu said that rather than dismissing criticism as coordinated attacks by competitors, Zhao should respond with facts and evidence.Xu was responding to a post questioning whether accounts defending Zhao were part of a bot network.The eight-episode drama stars Anthony Boyle as FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, Julia Garner as former Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison and Terry Chen as Zhao.Netflix did not respond to a request for comment.In an interview published by Netflix before the series' release, Graham Moore, the show's creator and co-showrunner, said he encouraged the actors to develop fully three-dimensional characters rather than simply imitate the real-life figures they portrayed.Speaking to Business Insider, Moore said, "I can never prove what was going on in the hearts or minds of Sam's friends when they made those decisions." Moore said he drew on extensive research into the real-life figures' backgrounds and public statements to imagine what may have driven the fractures between them."The story we're telling is not a financial story, and it's not a crypto story. It's a deeply personal story," he added.Netflix legal disputesWhile criticism of "The Altruists" has so far unfolded largely on social media, Netflix has previously faced defamation lawsuits over dramatizations of real-life events, including "Inventing Anna" and "Baby Reindeer."Rachel DeLoache Williams, a former Vanity Fair photo editor, sued Netflix in 2022 over her portrayal in "Inventing Anna," a series about convicted fraudster Anna Sorokin. Williams alleged that the show used her real name and personal details while falsely depicting her as greedy, dishonest and disloyal, including portraying her as exploiting her friendship with Sorokin for financial gain.The lawsuit was dismissed in February 2026 after the parties reached a settlement. Netflix and Williams' attorney reportedly confirmed the settlement in separate statements, saying, "Williams and Netflix have resolved the lawsuit."In 2024, Fiona Harvey, who said she inspired the character Martha in "Baby Reindeer," sued Netflix for at least $170 million. Harvey alleged that the series falsely portrayed her as a convicted stalker who had served time in prison and sexually assaulted the show's creator, Richard Gadd. The case is reportedly scheduled to go to trial in May 2027."We intend to defend this matter vigorously and to stand by Richard Gadd's right to tell his story," Netflix said in a statement reported by the Associated Press. She also challenged the show's claim to be based on a true story and alleged that viewers were able to identify her as the character depicted.

schema.headline: Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’ sparks FTX portrayal debate among crypto bigwigs from CZ to Star Xu

title: U.S. probes Megaspeed, Alice Huang as new figure emerges in Nvidia chip case
description: The logo of data center company Megaspeed International is pictured at its office in the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore on November 10, 2026. Tar
body: The logo of data center company Megaspeed International is pictured at its office in the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore on November 10, 2026. Taryn Ng | Afp | Getty ImagesThe U.S. is investigating Alice Huang and her former company, Megaspeed, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said, as a report identified one of her associates as a key decision-maker at the Singapore-based company.Clayton said the investigation was "ongoing" on Sunday, the day before Nvidia announced it had reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, a position he resigned from in part because of his relationship with Alice Huang.Alice Huang was a key figure in Megaspeed International, a cloud computing firm that operates data centers across Southeast Asia. U.S. intelligence reportedly believes she is a Chinese spy."There is an investigation ongoing into her firm and into her," Clayton told ABC on Sunday, adding that, "Nvidia chips, they are the jewel. They are the absolute top that everybody wants, that's why we're focusing on this."Nvidia's board announced Jensen Huang's return before the opening bell on Monday, saying it had "a series of discussions and meetings" with him.It added that it received input from senior levels of the United States government" and is confident that his reinstatement "poses no national security risk."President and CEO of Nvidia Jensen Huang speaks on AI at the return of American manufacturing at the Hill and Valley Forum at the U.S. Capitol on April 30, 2025 in Washington, DC.Kevin Dietsch | Getty ImagesAlice Huang's associate, Chinese national Li Ming, who is now out on bail in Singapore, was "deeply involved" in Megaspeed's activities and took part in major decisions, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Saturday, citing people familiar with the matter. The Singapore charges against Li concern alleged false representations to Super Micro Computer, a U.S.-based firm with known links to chipmaker Nvidia, though Megaspeed is not named in those charges.Last week, the Commerce and Justice departments said that the investigation into Megaspeed began in 2024 over potential export-control violations. Their joint statement said Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security and Singapore law enforcement interviewed Huang during an on-site check in June 2025. The Justice Department later took the lead in the criminal investigation.Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CBS on Sunday that the administration was seeking answers from Nvidia about its chip sales to China, including who oversaw compliance and which levels of the company knew about the activity.Separately, The New York Times reported Sunday that Alice Huang was in contact with an officer of a top Chinese intelligence agency from spring 2025 through fall 2026, citing people briefed on U.S. intelligence reports.Bloomberg reported last week that the Justice Department is investigating whether entities linked to Alice Huang helped smuggle Super Micro products to China.Li faces five charges in Singapore, including two counts of fraud by false representation, along with allegations involving the operation of a company he controlled, unauthorized bank-account access and another company director's duties. Prosecutors allege he falsely told Super Micro that the company would hold and lease the servers it purchased. The Journal reported that Li is out on bail and that his case is ongoing. He was offered bail of S$1 million in March 2025. The Singapore charges do not name Megaspeed.Earlier this month, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said that police had found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang committed offenses related to the possible inaccurate declarations under investigation. The ministry said she was issued a stern warning for providing information that police assessed as knowingly inaccurate and for downplaying her role at Megaspeed. It also said Singapore had not investigated her for espionage.Megaspeed has said it is a "legitimate and lawful business" and that Huang left the company in August 2025.Multiple smoking gunsThe scrutiny is set to intensify in Washington. Jensen Huang and the company's general counsel, Tim Teter, have agreed to closed-door, transcribed interviews with three House committees on Dec. 1 and Dec. 2, respectively. watch nowThe committees said they want answers about Nvidia's role in allowing Chinese actors to access advanced chips and the involvement of a potential Chinese intelligence asset.Speaking to CNBC's Squawk Box on Sunday U.S. time, Ryan Fedasiuk, a former advisor for U.S.-China Bilateral Affairs at the State Department, said that there was "still a lot we don't know" about the case. He said lawmakers would likely focus on Nvidia's customer relationships and "who knew what at the company when."Fedasiuk added that there was "a very good chance" investigators would find that people at Nvidia knew their products could be used for restricted purposes. He characterized the existing evidence as containing "multiple" smoking guns.

schema.headline: U.S. probes Megaspeed, Alice Huang as new figure emerges in Nvidia chip case

title: Trump tells CNBC ‘I made the deal’ to reinstate Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
description: watch nowPresident Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday morning that he spoke directly to Nvidia's board and urged them to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang."I s
body: watch nowPresident Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday morning that he spoke directly to Nvidia's board and urged them to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang."I spoke to them, let me put it that way," Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a phone interview shortly after Nvidia's shock announcement that Huang was returning to lead the tech giant."And I convinced them," the president said. "I made the deal."Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang came less than two weeks after he resigned. Huang had stepped down after admitting he cheated on his wife and amid claims his affairs included one with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees.Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, and her role as an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed raised concerns that she was facilitating the diversion of  Nvidia's most advanced semiconductor chip to China.Trump said Nvidia's board "did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said."And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot," the president said.Trump said that after he spoke with Nvidia's board, "when the deal was finished," he called Huang."I called him up, and I said: 'I ask you to do one thing, Jensen. Work hard,'" Trump said."I didn't talk about other things because he understands that. He understands it better than we do," the president said. "He knows what to do and what not to do. But I just said work hard because if you work hard, there's nobody that can capture what you've done. Nobody, nobody close."Trump also told CNBC that Huang "did nothing wrong."watch now"I think the [Nvidia] board acted really responsibly" in deciding to bring Huang back."People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president said. "I'm very, very happy that the company had the courage and the board had the courage to do the right thing, and they suffered for two weeks, and the company suffered greatly," the president said.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNvidia sharesAsked whether the broad stock market selloff last week after Huang's resignation from Nvidia factored into his decision to push for the CEO's reinstatement, Trump said, "Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term.""The bigger impact was, you know, he's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about," Trump said.This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.

schema.headline: Trump tells CNBC ‘I made the deal’ to reinstate Nvidia’s Jensen Huang

body: Vantor satellite image shows a vessel partly visible in the water beside a pier in Benghazi. Scattered debris and darkened areas are visible along the pier.Vantor | Vantor | Getty ImagesUkrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday lauded an "exemplary" military operation that sank one of Russia's newest ships at a Libyan port, after Kyiv's forces struck their target with several domestically made naval drones.The incident followed a suspected Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea on Saturday and occurred less than a week after damage was inflicted on Russian President Vladimir Putin's prized Crimea bridge.In a social media post, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces deployed seven sea drones to attack the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, at Benghazi's port in the early hours of Sunday morning. Ukraine's president posted dramatic video footage showing Ukraine's naval drones triggering a massive explosion on the Russian ship."Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk. It's one of their newest ships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale war," Zelenskyy said. "We continue our operations in designated waters," he added.Satellite imagery taken on Sunday showed the Merkury mostly underwater, having capsizedThe Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons, was hit by Ukrainian forces. A Ka-27 military helicopter on the Merkury was also destroyed.Asked about reports of attacks on Russian ships off the coast of Libya, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said information on this would be provided via the Defense Ministry. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky attends a press conference during a summit of the Coalition of the Willing for supporting Ukraine on November 19, 2026 in Berlin, Germany.Nadja Wohlleben | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesThe Security Service of Ukraine, the SBU, said Monday that the attacks "once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics have no safe routes even far beyond the Black Sea," according to a Google translation."Such unique special operations destroy the enemy's logistical capabilities and force Russia to pay for aggression even at a strategic distance from Ukraine," the SBU said via Telegram.'Serious concern'The United Nations Support Mission in Libya, or UNSMIL, expressed "serious concern" over the drone attacks in a statement saying the country "cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.""UNSMIL calls for an immediate, independent and transparent investigation to establish the facts and hold those responsible to account," it added. The incident is not the first time Libya has seen attacks linked to the Russia-Ukraine war near its territory. In March, Moscow's Transport Ministry accused Ukraine of striking the Arctic Metagaz, a liquefied natural gas tanker, as part of a suspected sea drone attack in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta.

schema.headline: Zelenskyy praises ‘exemplary’ drone operation that sank Russian warship in a Libyan port

title: Average 401(k), IRA balances fall as more workers raid their accounts, Fidelity says
description: watch nowRetirement account balances fell slightly in the third quarter amid market volatility, according to data released Monday from Fidelity Invest
body: watch nowRetirement account balances fell slightly in the third quarter amid market volatility, according to data released Monday from Fidelity Investments, the nation's largest provider of 401(k) savings plans.Some workers also tapped their retirement accounts for cash, signaling that persistent affordability pressures continue to strain household finances, said Mike Shamrell, Fidelity's vice president of thought leadership.The average 401(k) balance slipped 2% from the previous quarter to $152,500, while the average individual retirement account balance was down 1% to $142,261, Fidelity found. Both figures hit record highs during the second quarter. Despite the third-quarter decline, average balances in IRAs, 401(k)s and 403(b) plans — which are 401(k)-type plans offered by entities like public schools, churches and nonprofits — are higher year-over-year and continue to trend up over the long run.Wall Street's major averages finished the third quarter on mixed footing, driven in part by war with Iran, which blocked passage through the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit artery for global energy supplies, and caused oil prices to spike. The stock market's slowdown in the third quarter marked a cooling after the double-digit gains posted in the previous quarter. The S&P 500 index added 2.03% over the three-month period, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ended the quarter 2.2% higher.At the same time, financial pressures pushed more savers to reduce their contributions to retirement plans.The average 401(k) contribution rate, including employee and employer contributions, edged down to 14.3% from 14.4% in the second quarter, Fidelity found. Fidelity's recommended combined annual savings benchmark is 15%."We know that there is a lot of concern out there ... [and] people are likely making changes to their personal financial world," said Fidelity's Shamrell.Uptick in 401(k) loans, hardship withdrawalsSome savers also dipped into their accounts to free up cash, a sign of more acute financial strain amid persistently high prices and ongoing inflationary pressures.The share of workers with an outstanding loan in the third quarter was 19.6%, up slightly from 19.5% in the previous quarter, according to Fidelity. The percentage of participants taking a new loan from their 401(k) held steady at 2.8%.Separately, the share of workers taking a hardship withdrawal rose to 2.17% from 2.12% in the second quarter, Fidelity found.   "There is a rise because of economic reasons," said Philip Chao, a certified financial planner and chief investment officer at Experiential Wealth, based in Cabin John, Maryland. "No question about it."A hardship withdrawal can be taken from a retirement plan without paying an early-withdrawal penalty as long as the investor has an "immediate and heavy financial need," according to the IRS, such as avoiding foreclosure, eviction or unforeseen health expenses. Such distributions are also typically taxable.So-called leakage from 401(k) plans, particularly when workers cash out their accounts before retirement, can significantly erode long-term wealth by undermining the power of compound growth. Withdrawing funds during a market downturn can be especially damaging, making it more difficult to recover losses and benefit from a future rebound, financial advisors say."This is not a piggy bank," Chao said.However, despite the general consensus that savers shouldn't tap their retirement accounts, there may be situations in which investors don't have another good option, Chao said. In other words, the financial "ideal" doesn't align with "reality" for households, he said. watch nowA separate report issued this month by the Plan Sponsor Council of America, a trade group representing employers, found that the share of 401(k) participants with a loan outstanding from their workplace retirement plan rose "significantly" in 2025, nearly doubling from about 12% the prior year.The percentage of 401(k) investors who took a hardship withdrawal from their plan also increased for the third consecutive year, to 3.4% in 2025 from 1.5% in 2022, according to the PSCA report. Such "401(k) loans and hardships are there for participants when they need to tap the funds," said Hattie Greenan, the PSCA's research director. "Clearly there's a need right now."When a 401(k) withdrawal may be OK There are situations in which a retirement-plan withdrawal could be OK for workers, Chao said. For example, 401(k) loans are generally a cheaper form of borrowing than credit cards, because investors ultimately pay themselves back with interest, he said. "If you just need it for a month, two, three, that's fine," Chao said. "It's not going to kill you, borrowing from yourself."However, a 401(k) loan may make sense only if the saver believes they'll be able to repay it, he said. Failure to repay a loan can lead to income taxes and penalties that erode long-term savings, Chao said. Depending on the specific terms of a workplace retirement plan, investors who are laid off or leave their job may have to repay their full loan relatively quickly. Just 34% of plans allow for continued repayment of a loan after separation from service, according to the PSCA report. Subscribe to CNBC on YouTube.

schema.headline: Average 401(k), IRA balances fall as more workers raid their accounts, Fidelity says

title: Employees at Eric Trump-backed robot startup lose health benefits as company's cash crunch deepens
description: Foundation Future Industries, a start-up founded in 2024, aims to leverage humanoid robots for military and industrial work, rather than household tas
body: Foundation Future Industries, a start-up founded in 2024, aims to leverage humanoid robots for military and industrial work, rather than household tasks and the service sector.Foundation Future IndustriesEmployees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump.Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket."Because our last pay run through Rippling was in October, they have ended our benefits with them retroactive to October," a Foundation human resources manager said in the memo. "COBRA will be offered to all employees to cover November."Foundation has garnered headlines for the bold claims that co-founder Sankaet Pathak — whose previous startup collapsed in 2024 — has made about his robots and their potential use in war zones. Employees were last paid on Oct. 15, and some inside the company are angry at Pathak for a $4.6 million loan he took from his company last year, CNBC reported earlier this month.A Foundation spokesman didn't immediately respond to an email or phone call seeking comment. In the staff memo, Foundation blamed Rippling for the disruption to health coverage. The startup also said it would reimburse COBRA premiums paid by workers and that it was onboarding a new benefits provider. But employees, especially those whose family members are undergoing treatment for medical ailments, worry the company won't have funds to reimburse workers or reinstate coverage, people with direct knowledge of the situation said.In a statement to CNBC, Rippling indicated it was Foundation's failure to pay for its employee benefits that led to the change: "If a client enrolled in Rippling's [Professional Employer Organization] is unable to meet their payroll and benefits obligations for multiple months, they will first receive a warning and if not met, they are terminated."Rescue loanFoundation has been seeking a bridge loan to repay employees after its financial woes began in August. It has been in talks with three or four venture capital firms, including existing investor Tribe Capital, Pathak has told employees, according to people familiar with the situation, who asked to remain unnamed because they were not authorized to speak publicly and feared retaliation. Tribe didn't immediately return a request for comment. The bridge loan would help the company survive until a possible $150 million investment from South Korean conglomerate Base Group lands as early as December or January, Pathak has told employees, the people said.Base confirmed to Reuters in recent days that it was considering an investment, but the funding has not been finalized.Eric Trump, co-founder of World Liberty Financial, during the Token2049 conference in Singapore, on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Ore Huiying | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe potential investment would deepen business ties between the Trump family and the South Korean conglomerate, an aluminum producer also known for real estate and hospitality projects. Base paid the Trump Organization $2 million in 2025, according to a New York Times article, drawing scrutiny from Democratic senators over conflict-of-interest concerns. Base has also pursued other business relationships with the Trump Organization, including a Trump-branded golf course in South Korea. Eric Trump, who has invested in Foundation and was given the title of chief strategy advisor, didn't immediately respond to a CNBC email seeking comment. Inside FoundationThe prospect of employees having to pay for their own health coverage comes as many are already drawing down savings to cover living expenses. With another scheduled payday approaching on Nov. 30, workers are facing a third straight pay cycle without income.Many are actively interviewing for other jobs, and attendance at the company's San Francisco headquarters has fallen sharply, according to people familiar.Frustration has boiled over into distrust of Pathak's leadership for some employees, while others hope Pathak can secure funding to repay workers and bring the company back to financial health. In conversations and memos, Pathak says that he is highly invested in securing Foundation's future, the people said.Despite the firm's shaky finances, Foundation continued to hire for open roles until recently and some new workers have never been fully paid, said the people.To keep employees from leaving before a possible Base Group investment, Pathak has floated the idea of offering workers equity in the startup, the people said. At the same time, human resources staff have warned workers against taking legal action with California to recover their wages, saying that any employees who file complaints with the state would be dismissed, the people said. Following a Nov. 14 CNBC report detailing the missed payrolls and a $4.6 million loan Pathak took from the startup in 2025, the chief executive addressed the issue in an all-hands meeting, according to the people.Pathak defended the arrangement by telling workers that he had plowed his own money into the startup and takes only a nominal salary, the people said.The co-founder also told employees who were in dire financial straits to contact human resources for help covering personal bills, the people added."I'm burning through savings just to afford my apartment," one employee told CNBC. "It's extremely unfortunate we're in this situation."

schema.headline: Employees at Eric Trump-backed robot startup lose health benefits as company's cash crunch deepens

title: DNI Jay Clayton tapped as acting national cyber director
description: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testifies during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on threats to the homeland, in the Cannon H
body: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testifies during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on threats to the homeland, in the Cannon House Office Building in Washington, D.C., Nov. 18, 2026.Nathan Posner | Anadolu | Getty ImagesDirector of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has been tapped to serve as acting national cyber director while the Trump administration's permanent nominee for the role awaits Senate confirmation, a White House official told CNBC on Monday. Trump had already added artificial intelligence czar to Clayton's portfolio in October. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because the pick hasn't been announced.The White House last week announced that President Donald Trump had picked Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, to lead the Office of the National Cyber Director.The U.S. cyber director advises the president on cybersecurity and coordinates U.S. cyber policy across federal agencies. Federal law states that a person may not serve as an acting officer if the president has submitted that person's nomination to the Senate for full appointment and if that person served as first assistant to the office for less than 90 days.Davies would replace Sean Cairncross, who was confirmed to the role in August 2025 and whose departure was first reported by Axios last week.Trump, at a White House press conference on Friday, said he decided to replace Cairncross "because I didn't think that person was good enough."

schema.headline: DNI Jay Clayton tapped as acting national cyber director

title: Stuck: How a frozen housing market is hitting buyers, sellers and the economy
description: watch nowAutumn is usually a busy time in the housing market, but not this year. A sharp spike in mortgage rates in September has pushed the already c
body: watch nowAutumn is usually a busy time in the housing market, but not this year. A sharp spike in mortgage rates in September has pushed the already chilly real estate sector into a deep freeze. Buyers and sellers are moving to the sidelines, leaving those in the real estate business without much business.  It seems like everyone is stuck.The average rate on the popular 30-year fixed mortgage hovered around 6.60% in July, according to Mortgage News Daily. By the start of October, it was at 7.61%, a full percentage point higher."That shock, that rise of 100 basis points, is one of the fastest three-month increases we've seen in decades," said Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman on CNBC. While the jump in rates exacerbated the problem, the slowdown in the housing market has been building for years. Rising home prices have pushed the dream of homeownership out of reach for a growing number of Americans. The number of active buyers nationally has been declining for six straight months and in October hit its lowest level since the aftermath of the financial crisis, according to Redfin. The supply of homes for sale is also low. Builders are now faced with higher costs for land, labor, materials and energy. They simply can't afford to build the cheaper homes that are currently in demand. Single-family building permits, an indicator of future construction, were down 13% in October year over year, according to the U.S. Census. And builder sentiment in November dropped to the lowest level since 2012.A for sale sign is posted in front of a home for sale, Nov. 12, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesThis slowdown in the entire housing ecosystem is impacting every facet of Americans' lives and livelihoods."Where you live determines so much. It determines where your kids go to school. It determines the jobs that you have access to, right? It determines whether or not you're able to be close to your family," said Chen Zhao, chief economist at Redfin. "What we've seen with the housing market these past four years, with this historically low level of turnover, is that a lot of people really are stuck in their home."Closed sales of existing homes fell to a 16-year low in October, according to the National Association of Realtors. Pending sales, an indicator of future closings, hit a record low on the 25-year-old index from the Realtors.While the pace of home price increases has slowed recently, prices are up well over 50% from pre-pandemic levels. Part of that is because homebuilding has slowed to a crawl. 'The scary part'It all has Ryan Deighan, who wants to buy a home, wondering if he ever will."I genuinely don't know, and that's the scary part," he said.Deighan and his wife have been renting in Boston for six years. He is a chiropractor; she works in private equity. Even with a combined salary of more than $200,000 a year, he says they're stuck.Boston chiropractor Ryan Deighan is unsure if he'll ever be able to buy a home.CNBC"Making what I am and what my wife makes, it just feels like we're on paper doing well, but it feels like we are still kind of fighting to put down certain amounts toward a house," Deighan said.Being priced out of homeownership, he said, is changing what he called his "checklist" of how he once pictured his future."You graduate college, you find someone, you get married, you have the home with the white picket fence and the dog, and then the kids," he said. "That just looks a little different for us." Sellers are stuck, tooThe numbers don't just affect would-be buyers. They are hitting sellers, too. Robin Welch has been living in her Cleveland-area home for more than 20 years. Her children are now grown and moved out. She would like to downsize to a condominium, but the math doesn't make sense — in part, because her current interest rate is much lower than any new rate she could get. This has been dubbed the mortgage "lock-in effect.""It actually costs more money to buy less of a home," said Welch. "I would have to pay into an HOA, which would be another monthly expense on top of increased property taxes and increased interest rate."Welch has also done upgrades to her home over the years and doesn't want to have to start doing that on another home.Get Property Play directly to your inboxCNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.Subscribe here to get access today.Welch is part of why the housing turnover rate, which is how often homes get new owners, has now dropped to just 3.8% a year, well below the 5% rate in the decade following the financial crisis, according to Cotality.In addition, the national mobility rate, which is how often people move from region to region, has been falling for two years. It now sits at 8.3%, down from 11.1% a decade ago, according to Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies tabulations of U.S. Census Bureau data. Mobility hit a high of nearly 18% in the late 1980s."It's largely because of the interest lock-in effect, but also because of home prices just being so high," said Riordan Frost, senior research analyst at Harvard's JCHS. "Those things combined have made it hard both for existing homeowners to move and for people to get into homeownership." Americans have nearly $35 trillion of their wealth locked up in housing, a record high, according to Cotality. But the slowdown in the housing market, Frost said, impacts the accumulation, handover and use of that wealth. It also affects the labor market."Any kind of potential job would have to really outweigh … the price of taking that mortgage with a higher rate, or the price of moving, or the price of getting into a higher rent unit," Frost said.The wealth gap between homeowners and renters now is nothing short of massive. The most recent survey of consumer finances last year by the Federal Reserve showed that the median homeowner net wealth is about 43 times the median renter net wealth. "It has kind of knock-on effects for the rest of the economy. It has effects on the labor market and how good of a match we can get between employees and employers. It has an effect on education. It has an effect on just GDP growth," said Zhao.Buyers back out When homes aren't selling and people aren't moving, those who work in that business are stuck as well. The entire housing ecosystem is churning much more slowly, and the sudden jump in mortgage rates is causing deals to fall apart."Right after Labor Day, we went live with a bunch of listings. They all went under contract over the asking price," said Dana Bull, a real estate agent in the Boston suburbs. But then rates spiked. "It was a shock to the system," Bull said. "I think all of them came back on the market. We fell out of contract." Asked if she is seeing colleagues leaving the market, she answered: "People are thinking about it. It's tough."Dana Bull, a real estate agent in the Boston suburbs.CNBCThe economy has lost close to 2,000 jobs in real estate and leasing over the past year and 4,400 jobs in residential construction, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.Jobs in the mortgage industry have been falling since June and are down 38% since their last peak in the second quarter of 2021, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. That was when mortgage rates were less than half what they are today. Shant Banosian, president of Rate and the top mortgage originator in the U.S. by dollar volume, said his business is down about 30% this past year."Whenever change happens quickly, there's a slowdown," said Banosian, who has been in the business for 23 years. "It requires more of us to go out and advise, educate and guide. So, what I experienced was I just needed to spend more time on marketing, branding, relationship building. The conversations are longer because people want more information to try to navigate this market."Bull agrees. She said her job has gotten harder as well."We've done double the work this year, having homes go under contract, fall out of contract, putting them back under agreement, but definitely more negotiating," she said. "That's sort of my plea to both buyers and sellers: We need to get back to a space where we're comfortable negotiating."

schema.headline: Stuck: How a frozen housing market is hitting buyers, sellers and the economy

title: More Americans pay this Obama-era investment tax every year — how to avoid it
description: Former President Barack Obama speaks during an event to mark the 2010 passage of the Affordable Care Act in the East Room of the White House in Washin
body: Former President Barack Obama speaks during an event to mark the 2010 passage of the Affordable Care Act in the East Room of the White House in Washington, April 5, 2022.Chip Somodevilla | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesEvery year, more Americans pay an extra tax levy on their investment gains — but there's still time to reduce or avoid that bill for 2026, experts say. Net investment income tax, or NIIT, is a 3.8% levy on investment income once earnings exceed $200,000 for single filers or $250,000 for married couples filing jointly. The tax was enacted in 2010 under President Barack Obama to help fund healthcare via the Affordable Care Act. Unlike the federal income tax or capital gains brackets, the NIIT earnings limits don't adjust annually for inflation.As a result, "more clients get hit every year," said certified financial planner Michael Walstedt, founding advisor of Reliant Wealth Advisory in Hoboken, New Jersey. Roughly 5.6% of tax returns included NIIT for 2025, according to IRS data released in November for returns processed through mid-July 2026. That's up from about 3.7% for the same time frame in 2021. As more investors pay NIIT, here are some key things to know.How the net investment income tax works NIIT applies when you have investment income and your earnings exceed the modified adjusted gross income, or MAGI, limits, according to certified financial planner Marianela Collado, CEO of Tobias Financial Advisors in Plantation, Florida."The trick is to keep an eye on both of these numbers," said Collado, who is also a certified public accountant and member of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council.For the NIIT earnings limit, MAGI is typically the same as adjusted gross income, or AGI. One exception would be if you have foreign income, which changes the calculation. You can find last year's AGI on line 11a of your 2025 tax return. MAGI limits by filing statusMarried filing jointly: $250,000Married filing separately: $125,000Single: $200,000 Head of household (with qualifying person): $200,000Qualifying widow(er) with dependent child: $250,000NIIT applies to investment income, which includes interest, dividends, annuities, royalties, certain rents, and more. It can also include capital gains from a primary home sale, for profits that exceed the IRS exclusions. The exclusion is $250,000 for single filers or $500,000 for married couples.The levy stacks on top of regular income tax rates, or capital gains tax — which can be 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on earnings. That means higher earners can pay up to 23.8% on investment income, including long-term capital gains and NIIT.The NIIT calculation is 3.8% multiplied by the lesser of:net investment income, orthe amount that MAGI exceeds the income limits For example, if your MAGI is $30,000 above the NIIT earnings limit and you have $100,000 of investment income, you would pay 3.8% of $30,000, or $1,140.Alternatively, if your MAGI is $120,000 above the threshold and you have $100,000 of investment income, you would owe 3.8% of $100,000, or $3,800.How to avoid net investment income taxAs year-end approaches, investors should run projections to estimate their adjusted gross income, which can impact NIIT, among other tax consequences, experts say. If you're above the NIIT limits, you could reduce AGI by boosting pretax 401(k) deferrals or health savings account contributions, according to Collado with Tobias Financial Advisors.While employee 401(k) deferrals must happen by Dec. 31, you have until next year's tax deadline for health savings account contributions for 2026. You might also try to avoid selling assets before year-end, which could further boost AGI, experts say. Of course, any current-year tax moves should consider your long-term financial goals. watch nowAmid recent stock market volatility, investors may also consider so-called tax-loss harvesting, which uses losses to offset other portfolio gains, Walstedt with Reliant Wealth Advisory said. If your losses exceed profits, you can subtract up to $3,000 from regular income. After that, you can carry remaining losses into future tax years.However, if you're planning to reinvest the sale proceeds, you need to know the "wash sale rule," which blocks the tax-loss harvesting tax break for buying a "substantially identical" asset within 30 days before or after the sale.

schema.headline: More Americans pay this Obama-era investment tax every year — how to avoid it

title: Social Security benefits are rising in 2027, but other changes could affect what you keep
description: Halfpoint Images | Moment | Getty ImagesWhether you're working or retired, changes to Social Security in 2027 could affect your finances.Starting in J
body: Halfpoint Images | Moment | Getty ImagesWhether you're working or retired, changes to Social Security in 2027 could affect your finances.Starting in January, millions of program beneficiaries will get a 3.6% increase to their benefits, thanks to the annual cost-of-living adjustment. But rising Medicare premiums could chip away at the increase — and as beneficiaries' incomes rise, that may affect the taxes they owe and their eligibility for a new senior deduction.Meanwhile, a higher taxable earnings cap means some workers will pay Social Security taxes on more income, reducing their paycheck.Here's a breakdown of what to expect in the new year.Workers pay tax on more incomeSocial Security's limit for payroll taxes is adjusted every year to reflect the average wage index. In 2027, the taxable maximum will go up to $192,300 in earnings, up from $184,500 in 2026. Workers and employers each pay a 6.2% payroll tax on earnings up to that limit — or 12.4% for self-employed workers. Medicare taxes of 1.45% for both workers and employers are not subject to a limit.In 2027, workers who earn $192,300 or more will pay $11,922.60 in total Social Security payroll taxes, according to the Social Security Administration, while self-employed workers will pay $23,845.20. "If you're somebody whose income is over what the new threshold is going to be, this increase in the threshold results in a tax increase to you," said Tim Steffen, director of advanced planning at financial services firm Baird. The COLA boostThe 3.6% Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 is slated to increase retirement benefits by about $75 per month on average, according to the Social Security Administration. The annual adjustment is the largest boost to benefits since 2023 due to rising inflation. The COLA averaged 2.6% from 2000 to 2026, according to the Senior Citizens League, a nonpartisan senior group.Around 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see benefit increases, according to the agency. The maximum benefit for a worker at full retirement age — when individuals become eligible for 100% of the benefits they've earned — will rise to $4,188 per month in 2027, up from $4,152 per month in 2026, according to the federal agency. To be eligible for the maximum benefit at full retirement age — typically age 66 to 67 — you generally have to earn up to the taxable threshold for each of your working years factored into the calculation.Rising Medicare costsMomo Productions | Digitalvision | Getty ImagesHow much of the COLA increase Social Security beneficiaries see depends in part on their Medicare premiums, which may be deducted directly from benefit checks.Monthly rates are poised to increase for both Medicare Part B, which covers medically necessary services and preventive care, and Part D, which provides prescription drug coverage. The standard monthly Medicare Part B premium will be $209.40 in 2027 — a $6.50 increase from $202.90 in 2026, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services."It's not often that we see a Part B [premium] increase that is lower than the COLA," Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare policy analyst, said of the 3.2% increase. The last time that happened was in 2023, she said.Medicare Part D beneficiaries may also pay higher premiums in 2027.Assuming enrollees keep the same plan, the average enrollment-weighted monthly Part D premium may be $51 in 2027, up 50% from $34 in 2026, according to projections from KFF, a provider of health policy research and polling. That is higher than CMS' projections, which forecast the national average premium for standalone Part D plans will rise about $1, to $36, in 2027 from $35 in 2026. Standard monthly premiums for Part B and plan-specific premiums for Part D apply to individuals who have $112,000 or less in modified adjusted gross income, or $224,000 for married couples. Beneficiaries with higher income pay larger premiums because of income-related monthly adjustment amounts, which affect 9% of Medicare Part B and Part D beneficiaries, according to CMS. Taxes on benefitsWith bigger Social Security benefits, more households may find that some portion of benefits is taxable — though a new senior deduction may help provide some relief to those who are eligible.Social Security benefits may be subject to federal income taxes for certain individuals. The thresholds at which those taxes are applied are not adjusted from year to year. Whether or not benefits are taxed is determined by a formula known as combined income — the sum of adjusted gross income, tax-exempt interest income and half of Social Security benefits:Individuals with less than $25,000 in combined income — and married couples with less than $32,000 — pay no taxes on their benefit income.Up to 50% of benefits are taxable for individuals with between $25,000 and $34,000 in combined income, or for married couples with $32,000 and $44,000.Up to 85% of benefits are taxable for individuals with more than $34,000 in combined income and for married couples with over $44,000. Individuals who are subject to taxes may opt to withhold taxes from their Social Security benefit checks, rather than face a potential bill during tax filing season.Separately, a temporary senior deduction of up to $6,000 for individuals ages 65 and over may help to indirectly reduce taxes on Social Security benefits.That deduction, part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025, helps reduce retirees' taxable income, according to Steffen. It's in place through 2028. Because the break phases out for individuals with modified adjusted gross income starting at $75,000 — and for married couples with $150,000 — it's important to watch your income if you're close to those limits, Steffen said."Keep in mind that if you're over 65, you might qualify for this deduction," Steffen said. "But if you let your income get too big, you might lose the deduction."Moreover, any extra income that causes you to lose the deduction may also come with its own taxes, making it more expensive, according to Steffen."What we've been telling our clients is that tax planning is a lot more complicated than it used to be, and you can't do it on the back of an envelope anymore," he said. "You need to use good tools that can do good calculations for you."Benefit withholdings for workersRainstar | E+ | Getty ImagesIndividuals who claim Social Security retirement benefits before their full retirement age and who continue to work may be subject to withholdings.In 2027, individuals under full retirement age may earn up to $25,560 per year, up from $24,480 in 2026, without adjustments to their Social Security benefits. For every $2 in earnings above that limit, $1 in Social Security benefits will be withheld.Importantly, those withholdings are not lost completely. Once a beneficiary reaches full retirement age, the withheld money will be credited to their benefits over their remaining lifespan.In the year individuals reach full retirement age, the retirement earnings test limit is higher — $67,920 per year in 2027, up from $65,160 per year in 2026. For every $3 in earnings above that limit, $1 in Social Security benefits is withheld.Starting the month a beneficiary reaches full retirement age, no earnings are withheld.

schema.headline: Social Security benefits are rising in 2027, but other changes could affect what you keep
